newsitem.title: JAPAN: WEEK AHEAD - Tokyo stocks seen attempting a rebound.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - Tokyo stocks seen attempting a rebound.

text.p: Tokyo stocks are likely to try to rebound in the week ahead but feeble market sentiment may stunt any rebound, brokers said.
Stocks suffered a losing streak in the past week that brought a total loss exceeding four percent.

"Technical alarms are beginning to clang signalling that the index is being oversold, so further falls should be limited," said Harushige Kobayashi, deputy general manager at Yamaichi Securities. "But the investor mood is so chilly, gains may be hard to accumulate."
Most market sources said the Nikkei 225 was likely to be locked in a 20,500 to 21,500 range, with the benchmark toeing the downside.
The key Nikkei benchmark of 225 selected issues shed 263.52 points or 1.25 percent to end at 20,739.97 on Friday, closing below the 21,000 threshold for the first time in two weeks.
The benchmark's losses ballooned to over 870 points for the week. The last time it recorded a five-session losing streak was in July. Between July 4 and July 10 it shed about 600 points.

"The Nikkei average is sagging near the bottom of the 20,500 to 21,500 box and institutional investor buying is beginning to pick up," said Nobuhiro Kaneda, general manager at Daiwa Securities. "Rather than falling, the benchmark will try to consolidate in the coming week as investors move to buy shares of firms whose earnings outlook is bright."
However, some market sources said political uncertainties would continue to hinder trade.

Before the general election on October 20, investors and dealers snapped up shares, pushing the Nikkei average up more than 640 points, confident the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) stood a good chance of clinching an overall majority.
But the party, the dominant partner in the previous coalition, fell 12 seats short of a Lower House majority.

"Some investors, including many foreign investors, think that economic and political reform will be a long process ... and the market mood will continue to be depressed," said Kiyoshi Kimura at Societe Generale Securities.
